question.problem: Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\end{aligned}
$$
